svg.aria-label: How to write मम नाम: 2 words, मम, नाम, one after another
svg.title: Writing मम नाम
svg.desc: 2 words written one after another: मम, नाम (devanagari). Each word is drawn as its letters' bodies in reading order, then one headline over that word; the space between words breaks the headline. Each word has its own group of frames; frame N of a group shows movements 1 to N of that word, the movement being added drawn in ink over the finished word, whose outline is read from _fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Static.ttf. Each word is drawn at its own scale from its own cited stroke order, so the strip does not show how large the words are next to each other, how far apart they sit, or any join between them. Stroke order: मम: letters 1 and 2: JackPotte, ‘Devanagari m म.gif’, strokes 1–3, Wikimedia Commons, 29 March 2009; the shared headline, drawn last: HP Labs India, Lipi Toolkit, Lipi Indic Character Recognizers 4.0, Devanagari recognizer: native writers' stored prototypes of the 33 consonants draw the headline as the last stroke in 82% of 2,706 and as the first in about 5% (MIT licence, 2012) <https://lipitk.sourceforge.net/lipi-reco.htm>; नाम: letter 1: Opiaterein, ‘Deva-न-order.gif’, strokes 1–3, Wikimedia Commons, 11 May 2009; sign 2: HP Labs India, Lipi Toolkit, Lipi Indic Character Recognizers 4.0, Devanagari recognizer, class 47 (ा, aa sign): stored online-handwriting prototypes from native writers (MIT licence, 2012); letter 3: JackPotte, ‘Devanagari m म.gif’, strokes 1–3, Wikimedia Commons, 29 March 2009; the place of sign 2, after its consonant's body: Saurmandal, ‘Devanagari आ stroke order.svg’, frames 1–5, Wikimedia Commons, 5 August 2023; the shared headline, drawn last: HP Labs India, Lipi Toolkit, Lipi Indic Character Recognizers 4.0, Devanagari recognizer: native writers' stored prototypes of the 33 consonants draw the headline as the last stroke in 82% of 2,706 and as the first in about 5% (MIT licence, 2012) <https://lipitk.sourceforge.net/lipi-reco.htm>. Source notes on variation: मम: The letters are drawn in reading order, each as its own cited strip draws it but without its own headline, placed where the bundled font prints it in the word: letters 1 and 2 after JackPotte, ‘Devanagari m म.gif’, strokes 1–3, Wikimedia Commons, 29 March 2009 <https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Devanagari_m_%E0%A4%AE.gif>. Each letter's own note on variation is printed with that letter's own strip. The headline is then drawn once, left to right, over the whole word. That is the order most native writers use for a single letter: in HP Labs India's LipiTk 4.0 Devanagari recognizer the stored prototypes of the 33 consonants draw the headline last in 82% of 2,706 and first in about 5%. It is a majority, not a rule: some writers draw the headline first. The traces are single letters, so carrying their order across a word is this book's reading of them; no reachable source records native writers' headline timing in whole words. नाम: The letters are drawn in reading order, each as its own cited strip draws it but without its own headline, placed where the bundled font prints it in the word: letter 1 after Opiaterein, ‘Deva-न-order.gif’, strokes 1–3, Wikimedia Commons, 11 May 2009 <https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Deva-%E0%A4%A8-order.gif>; sign 2 after HP Labs India, Lipi Toolkit, Lipi Indic Character Recognizers 4.0, Devanagari recognizer, class 47 (ा, aa sign): stored online-handwriting prototypes from native writers (MIT licence, 2012) <https://lipitk.sourceforge.net/lipi-reco.htm>; letter 3 after JackPotte, ‘Devanagari m म.gif’, strokes 1–3, Wikimedia Commons, 29 March 2009 <https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Devanagari_m_%E0%A4%AE.gif>. Each letter's own note on variation is printed with that letter's own strip. The place of sign 2, after its consonant's body and before the headline, after Saurmandal, ‘Devanagari आ stroke order.svg’, frames 1–5, Wikimedia Commons, 5 August 2023 <https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Devanagari_%E0%A4%86_stroke_order.svg>; the sign's own piece of headline becomes part of the word's one headline. The cited आ is अ with the ā bar after it: its buildup frames draw the body, then (frame 4) the trailing stem top-to-bottom, then (frame 5) the shirorekhā left-to-right. The book draws the ā sign the same way on a consonant: the consonant's body, then the stem, then the headline across both. Native writers agree for आ: of the 83 prototypes of आ stored in HP Labs India's LipiTk 4.0 Devanagari recognizer, 52 (63%) are body strokes, then the bar, then the headline; the bar comes after the body in 69% and before the headline in 65% (the data is licensed for research use only, so only shares are cited). KanoAI's hand-made Gujarati barakhadi templates draw ા after its consonant in all 32 rows that keep the consonant's bare outline, in a script with no headline. No reachable source records native writers' consonant + ā syllables (HP Labs India's hpl-dvng-iso-word set, which would, is on a host the authoring environment cannot reach), so carrying आ's order to the sign on a consonant is this book's reading of that evidence, at medium confidence. Handwriting varies by writer. The headline is then drawn once, left to right, over the whole word. That is the order most native writers use for a single letter: in HP Labs India's LipiTk 4.0 Devanagari recognizer the stored prototypes of the 33 consonants draw the headline last in 82% of 2,706 and first in about 5%. It is a majority, not a rule: some writers draw the headline first. The traces are single letters, so carrying their order across a word is this book's reading of them; no reachable source records native writers' headline timing in whole words.
svg.text: How it is written — 2 words, one after another
Word 1 of 2 — 3 strokes · 2 pen lifts · 7 movements
Word 2 of 2 — 5 strokes · 4 pen lifts · 7 movements
Word 1: stroke order after letters 1 and 2: JackPotte, ‘Devanagari m म.gif’, strokes 1–3, Wikimedia Commons, 29 March 2009; the shared headline, drawn last: HP Labs India, Lipi
Toolkit, Lipi Indic Character Recognizers 4.0, Devanagari recognizer: native writers' stored prototypes of the 33 consonants draw the headline as the last stroke in 82% of 2,706 and
as the first in about 5% (MIT licence, 2012)
Word 2: stroke order after letter 1: Opiaterein, ‘Deva-न-order.gif’, strokes 1–3, Wikimedia Commons, 11 May 2009; sign 2: HP Labs India, Lipi Toolkit, Lipi Indic Character
Recognizers 4.0, Devanagari recognizer, class 47 (ा, aa sign): stored online-handwriting prototypes from native writers (MIT licence, 2012); letter 3: JackPotte, ‘Devanagari m
म.gif’, strokes 1–3, Wikimedia Commons, 29 March 2009; the place of sign 2, after its consonant's body: Saurmandal, ‘Devanagari आ stroke order.svg’, frames 1–5, Wikimedia Commons, 5
August 2023; the shared headline, drawn last: HP Labs India, Lipi Toolkit, Lipi Indic Character Recognizers 4.0, Devanagari recognizer: native writers' stored prototypes of the 33
consonants draw the headline as the last stroke in 82% of 2,706 and as the first in about 5% (MIT licence, 2012)
This order is attested, not standardised; the source records where it varies.
